etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gasen; akin to Swedish dialectal gasa and Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (usgaisjan, “to terrify”).

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 1:11:
quote.text: Why stand ye gazing up into heaven?

quote.citation: 1922 February, James Joyce, “[Episode 13]”, in Ulysses, Paris: Shakespeare and Company, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Gerty MacDowell who was seated near her companions, lost in thought, gazing far away into the distance was, in very truth, as fair a specimen of winsome Irish girlhood as one could wish to see.

quote.citation: 1936, F.J. Thwaites, The Redemption, Sydney: H. John Edwards Publishing, published 1940, page 64:
quote.text: She just sat there very straight, gazing across the moon-washed garden.

quote.citation: 1998, Michelangelo Antonioni, Unfinished Business: Screenplays, Scenerios, and Ideas, page xv:
quote.text: In fact, for Antonioni this gazing is probably the most fundamental of all cognitive activities[.]

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VII”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Strait toward Heav'n my wondring Eyes I turnd, / And gaz'd a while the ample Skie

quote.citation: 1970, David Bowie, The Man Who Sold the World:
quote.text: I searched for form and landFor years and years I roamedI gazed a gazeless stare.

definitions.definition: A fixed look; a look of eagerness, wonder, or admiration; a continued look of attention.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, “A Lady in Company”, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Captain Edward Carlisle, soldier as he was, martinet as he was, felt a curious sensation of helplessness seize upon him as he met her steady gaze, her alluring smile; he could not tell what this prisoner might do.

quote.citation: 1609, William Shakespeare, “Sonnet 5”, in Shake-speares Sonnets. […], London: By G[eorge] Eld for T[homas] T[horpe] and are to be sold by William Aspley, →OCLC:
quote.text: Those howers that with gentle worke did frame / The louely gaze where euery eye doth dwell.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “Samson Agonistes, […].”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 11:
quote.text: Made of my Enemies the ſcorn and gaze;

definitions.definition: (psychoanalysis) In Lacanian psychoanalysis, the relationship of the subject with the desire to look and awareness that one can be viewed.

quote.citation: 2003, Amelia Jones, The feminism and visual culture reader, page 35:
quote.text: She counters the tendency to focus on critical strategies of resisting the male gaze, raising the issue of the female spectator.
